introduction-schrodingers-backup.core: A backup you've never restored is both valid and broken until you try it. You don't have backups, you have restores, so a DBRE proves recovery with scheduled, automated restore drills.

first_principles.problem: Backup jobs go green for years. Then disaster strikes and the files turn out to be empty, truncated, encrypted with a lost key, or take three weeks to restore when the business needed three hours. Nobody ever ran the restore.
truths: A successful backup job proves only that a file was written.
Failures hide until you read the file back.
derivation: Treat the **restore** as the real product, not the backup.
**Restore regularly** into an isolated environment.
**Validate** the restored data, not just the exit code.
**Time** it, so you know your real recovery time.

analogy.title: The spare tyre you never checked
analogy.story: You feel safe with a spare in the boot, but if you've never checked its pressure, you'll find out it's flat exactly when you have a puncture on the motorway.
analogy.breaks: A tyre check takes a minute. A full restore of a big database takes hours, which is exactly why you must measure it before you need it.

example.title: "How do you know your backups work?"
example.scenario: An interview question, and a real incident question.

steps.label: Strong answer
steps.detail: "We restore automatically every week into isolation, run data checks, and track the duration against RTO."

example.outcome: confidence based on evidence, not hope.

check.q: Why is a successful backup exit code not enough?
check.a: It doesn't prove the file is complete, readable, decryptable or restorable within the time the business needs.

logical-backups-the-portable-approach.core: A logical backup (pg_dump, mysqldump) exports data as SQL or rows, so it's portable across versions and selective per table, but restores are slow (every row and index rebuilt) and it's only a snapshot, with no point-in-time recovery.

first_principles.problem: We need copies of data that can move between database versions, be inspected, or restore just one table. Raw binary files can't do that.
truths: SQL statements describe data independently of storage format.
Replaying statements and rebuilding indexes takes time.
A dump captures one moment only.
derivation: Export **meaning, not bytes**: `CREATE` and `INSERT` statements, or a compressed custom format (`pg_dump -Fc`).
Restore by re-executing, with **parallel workers** (`pg_restore -j 4`) to speed it up.
Use it for **major-version upgrades, migrations and single-table restores**.
Accept **slow restores** at TB scale, **no PITR**, and scan load on production while dumping.

analogy.title: Retyping a book from a transcript
analogy.story: A logical backup is a full transcript of the book. Anyone can retype it in any typeface or format (portable), and you can retype just chapter 3. But retyping a 10,000-page book takes a very long time.
analogy.breaks: Transcribing a book doesn't disturb its readers. pg_dump reads every page and can evict hot data from the buffer cache, so run it off a replica if possible.

example.title: Upgrading Postgres 13 → 16
example.scenario: Physical files can't move between major versions.

steps.label: Dump
steps.detail: Custom-format dump, ideally from a replica.

steps.label: Restore
steps.detail: Parallel restore into the new major version.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Row counts and spot checks before cutover.

code.text:
pg_dump -Fc -d app -f app.dump
createdb -h pg16 app
pg_restore -h pg16 -d app -j 4 app.dump

example.outcome: data moves cleanly across a version boundary that binary backups can't cross.

check.q: Why can't a logical backup give you the state at 10:42:17?
check.a: It's a snapshot of one moment (when the dump ran). There's no change log to replay to an arbitrary second.

physical-backups-the-speed-demons.core: A physical backup copies the database's raw files (base backup) and continuously archives WAL. Restores are fast and support point-in-time recovery, but backups are tied to the same major version and usually restore whole clusters.

first_principles.problem: Re-executing millions of INSERTs and rebuilding indexes can take days at terabyte scale, far beyond any reasonable recovery time. And snapshots alone can't recover to the second before a mistake.
truths: Copying files is much faster than replaying SQL.
The WAL records every change in order.
Binary formats are specific to versions and platforms.
derivation: Take a periodic **base backup** of the data directory (pgBackRest, WAL-G, XtraBackup).
Turn on **archive_mode** and ship every WAL segment off-site with `archive_command`.
Restore = copy the base, then **replay WAL**, which gives fast recovery and **PITR**.
Accept: **same major version only**, mostly **all-or-nothing**, more **operational setup**.
Use **both**: physical for disaster recovery, logical for migrations and single tables.

analogy.title: Photocopying the pages vs. retyping the book
analogy.story: A physical backup is a perfect photocopy of every page, which is fast to reproduce. Keep a diary of every edit made since (WAL), and you can recreate the book exactly as it was at any moment. But the photocopies only fit the same binder (version).
analogy.breaks: Photocopies are instant to read. Replaying WAL is fast but not instant, so days of WAL since the last base backup still take hours to apply.

example.title: Setting up WAL-G to S3
example.scenario: Production Postgres: nightly base backups plus continuous WAL.

steps.label: WAL
steps.detail: Every finished WAL segment is pushed to S3 within seconds.

steps.label: Base
steps.detail: A nightly base backup bounds how much WAL a restore must replay.

steps.label: Restore
steps.detail: Fetch the base, replay WAL, recover to any second in the window.

code.text:
# postgresql.conf
archive_mode    = on
archive_command = 'wal-g wal-push %p'
# cron: wal-g backup-push $PGDATA   (nightly)

example.outcome: recovery measured in hours instead of days, to any chosen second.

check.q: When would you still use a logical backup?
check.a: For major-version upgrades, cross-platform migrations, or restoring a single table.

point-in-time-recovery-pitr-mechanics.core: PITR restores the last base backup and replays archived WAL up to a chosen moment (e.g. one second before a DROP TABLE), then promotes. It only works if the WAL archive has no gaps.

first_principles.problem: Someone runs `DROP TABLE users;` at 10:00:00 and it's noticed at 10:05. Restoring last night's backup loses ten hours of orders and sign-ups. We need the state at 09:59:59.
truths: The base backup is a known-good starting point.
WAL replays every change in order.
Replay can stop at any timestamp.
derivation: **Fetch the base backup** from before the target time.
**Download WAL** from the base up to the target.
**Replay** in order and **stop at `recovery_target_time`**.
**Promote** to read-write.
Guard the **WAL retention window** and **archive continuity**: a missing segment stops replay at that gap.

analogy.title: Rewinding a recorded game
analogy.story: Load last night's saved game, then fast-forward the recording of every move and stop the instant before the fatal mistake. If a chunk of the recording is missing, you can't fast-forward past it.
analogy.breaks: A game recording is tiny. WAL for a busy database can be hundreds of GB per day, so replay time is often the biggest part of recovery.

example.title: Undoing DROP TABLE at 10:00:00
example.scenario: Base backup at midnight, WAL archived continuously.

steps.label: Isolate
steps.detail: Restore onto a new server so production keeps running.

steps.label: Target
steps.detail: Stop at 09:59:59, one second before the drop.

steps.label: Recover
steps.detail: Copy the `users` table back into production.

code.text:
# on the restore server (PostgreSQL 12+), plus an empty recovery.signal file
restore_command      = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-10-11 09:59:59+00'

example.outcome: ten hours of data saved. Only the mistake is undone.

points: Base + WAL replay to a target time.
Restore beside production, then copy back.
WAL gaps break PITR, so monitor the archive.

check.q: Why is WAL archive monitoring as important as the backup itself?
check.a: A single missing segment stops replay at that point, silently removing PITR for everything after it.

rto-vs-rpo-defining-success-before-disas.core: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose, and it sets backup frequency. RTO is how long you can be down, and it sets the restore mechanism. Agree both with the business before an incident, and prove them by measuring.

first_principles.problem: Without targets, every incident becomes a negotiation under pressure: "how long will this take?" while the CEO is on the phone. Teams often compute RPO correctly but never time a restore, then discover recovery takes 36 hours against a 4-hour expectation.
truths: Data written since the last safe copy can be lost.
Restore time depends on data size and mechanism.
Targets agreed in calm beat guesses made in a crisis.
derivation: **RPO** (time of data loss): daily dump ≈ 24 h, hourly ≈ 1 h, continuous WAL ≈ seconds.
**RTO** (time to recover): 10 TB via pg_dump is 24–72 h, physical parallel restore 2–6 h, standby failover seconds to minutes.
Let RPO pick **backup frequency** and RTO pick **restore architecture**.
Close the **dangerous gap**: measure actual restore time with drills.

analogy.title: Saving your work
analogy.story: RPO is how often you press Ctrl+S: save every hour and a crash can cost you an hour of work. RTO is how long it takes to get back to work after the crash: reboot, reopen, reload. Fast saving doesn't help if your computer takes a day to reboot.
mapping: Time to get back to work
analogy.breaks: Your laptop's reboot time is constant. Restore time grows as data grows, so an RTO met last year may be missed this year.

example.title: A 5 TB database with RTO 2 h
example.scenario: The team relies on nightly pg_dump.

steps.label: Mismatch
steps.detail: pg_dump can't meet a 2-hour RTO at 5 TB, however reliable the dumps are.

steps.label: Redesign
steps.detail: Physical backups plus WAL for RPO in seconds, and a warm standby for RTO in minutes.

example.outcome: targets drive architecture, and measurements prove the architecture meets them.

check.q: Which mechanism is needed for an RTO of seconds?
check.a: A warm standby replica you can fail over to. Restoring from backup always takes far longer.

designing-a-restore-drill-what-tested-ac.core: A real restore drill answers three questions: did it restore, is the data correct, and is it usable? It runs automatically, in isolation, on a schedule, and reports duration, freshness and check results over time.

first_principles.problem: "The restore command exited 0" isn't proof. Data can be silently missing, stale or broken. Drills that need a human get skipped exactly when things are busiest, which is when backup hygiene drifts.
truths: Restore time trends upward as data grows.
derivation: Check three things: **completion, data integrity, application usability**.
Restore into an **isolated** environment, with production-grade security, and **tear it down** afterwards.
**Automate** the five steps: fetch, start, validate, report, teardown. Weekly at least, daily for critical systems.
**Report** duration (vs RTO), freshness (vs RPO), check results, and the **trend**.

analogy.title: A real fire drill vs. a checklist
analogy.story: Ticking "fire exits exist" on a form isn't a drill. A drill means everyone actually walks out, someone times it, someone counts heads, and the results are compared with last time.
analogy.breaks: Fire drills don't involve sensitive data. A restored database contains production data, so the drill environment needs encryption, access control and teardown.

example.title: A weekly automated drill
example.scenario: Critical orders database. RTO 2 h, RPO 5 min.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Row counts per table vs production stats, foreign key spot checks, and the latest `created_at` within 5 minutes of the target.

steps.label: Usability
steps.detail: Run a few real application queries against the restored DB.

steps.label: Trend
steps.detail: Restore time went 70 → 85 → 98 minutes over 3 months, so act before it crosses 120.

code.text:
t0=$(date +%s)
wal-g backup-fetch "$PGDATA" LATEST && touch "$PGDATA/recovery.signal"
pg_ctl -D "$PGDATA" -o "-p 6543" -w start
psql -p 6543 -f checks.sql > report.txt
echo "restore_seconds=$(( $(date +%s) - t0 ))" >> report.txt
pg_ctl -D "$PGDATA" stop && rm -rf "$PGDATA"

example.outcome: recoverability is proven every week, and slow drift towards an RTO breach is visible months ahead.

check.q: Why track restore duration over time?
check.a: Data grows, so restores get slower. A rising trend warns you before you actually breach your RTO.
